summary: 12 finding(s) across 5 file(s): 2 blocker, 1 high, 6 medium, 3 low, 0 info. 4 rule(s) depend on APIs missing from your QNX SDP 8.0.0 sysroot. Detected roles: device service, periodic control loop, daemon. Recommended shape on QNX: a /dev/motor_pid resource manager driven by a pulse timer. Readiness score 0/100 (deterministic formula).

findings.title: epoll event loop

locations.snippet: if (cfd >= 0) { ev.data.fd = cfd; epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, cfd, &ev); }

findings.guidance: epoll is a Linux-only readiness API. On QNX use POSIX poll()/select() for the lowest-effort port, or restructure the loop around a channel so I/O readiness (ionotify), timers and IPC all arrive as prioritized pulses on one receive call.

alternatives.note: Lowest effort and portable. Keeps the existing loop shape.
One receive loop for I/O readiness, timers and IPC, served in priority order.

findings.sysroot_detail: epoll_wait: not exported by any sysroot library; <sys/epoll.h> not in sysroot

findings.title: timerfd periodic timer
findings.guidance: Use a POSIX timer created with timer_create(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) whose sigevent is a pulse (SIGEV_PULSE_INIT) delivered to a channel. The receiving thread blocks in MsgReceivePulse() and wakes at the pulse priority you choose. For a simple loop, clock_nanosleep(TIMER_ABSTIME) avoids drift.

alternatives.note: Periodic pulse timer: priority-aware, no fd needed.
Absolute-time sleep loop; simplest drift-free option.

findings.sysroot_detail: timerfd_create: not exported by any sysroot library; <sys/timerfd.h> not in sysroot

findings.title: Linux /sys paths
findings.guidance: There is no sysfs on QNX. PWM, GPIO and thermal data come from board-specific resource managers. Hide these behind a HAL and implement the QNX backend for your board's drivers.

findings.title: Host-only compiler settings
findings.guidance: Cross-compile with qcc/q++ and a -V variant (gcc_ntox86_64, gcc_ntoaarch64le). Remove host-only flags such as -march=native and hardcoded gcc, and do not fail the build when CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME is not Linux. The kit's toolchain file sets all of this.

findings.title: sched_setaffinity
findings.guidance: On QNX pin threads with run-masks: ThreadCtl(_NTO_TCTL_RUNMASK_GET_AND_SET_INHERIT, ...) sets the calling thread's mask and the mask its children inherit.
findings.sysroot_detail: sched_setaffinity: not exported by any sysroot library

findings.title: ioctl on device descriptors

locations.snippet: ioctl(enc_fd, TIOCMBIS, &bits);       /* wake the encoder bridge */

findings.guidance: QNX offers ioctl() as a wrapper over devctl() for common requests, but driver-specific requests must be rewritten against the QNX driver's DCMD_* set. Wrap device access in a small hardware-abstraction layer (HAL) so the Linux and QNX implementations can live side by side.

alternatives.note: Driver-specific DCMD_* commands; check the driver for your board.
Introduce a HAL interface around device access.

findings.title: Linux-only link libraries
findings.guidance: On QNX the pthread, real-time and dynamic-loading functions are part of libc. Drop a -l flag only if that library is missing from the sysroot (the audit checks this). In CMake prefer find_package(Threads) + Threads::Threads.
findings.sysroot_detail: not in sysroot lib dirs: libpthread, librt (provided by libc on QNX)

findings.title: Mutex without priority inheritance in mixed-priority code
findings.guidance: A mutex shared between threads of different priorities should use PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT so a low-priority holder is boosted while a high-priority thread waits. QNX message passing already applies client-priority inheritance by default, which is one reason to move shared state behind a resource manager.

alternatives.note: Explicit priority inheritance on the shared mutex.
Message passing inherits the client's priority.

findings.title: systemd unit / watchdog script

locations.snippet:
[Unit]
Description=Motor PID controller (1 kHz)
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/motor_pid /etc/motor-pid/gains.conf
Restart=always
RestartSec=1
CPUSchedulingPolicy=fifo
CPUSchedulingPriority=80
WatchdogSec=2

findings.guidance: QNX targets have no systemd. Start the service from the image's startup script (or SLM where available), daemonize with procmgr_daemon(), and supervise daemon processes using procmgr_event_notify_add(PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH, ...) (or HAM where the optional High Availability package is installed).

alternatives.note: Process manager daemon death notifications and supervisor restart loop.

findings.title: Background threads next to a real-time loop
findings.guidance: Adaptive partitioning (APS) is not part of QNX SDP 8.0. To bound a background thread's CPU use, run it under SCHED_SPORADIC (budget + replenishment period), watch its per-thread CPU-time clock with a timer to detect overruns, pin it away from the control core with a run-mask, or use the QNX Hypervisor for hard isolation.

findings.title: inotify file watching
findings.guidance: QNX 8.0 provides <sys/inotify.h>. Link with -lfsnotify and make sure the fsevmgr service runs on the target. This is a build-flag change, not a blocker.

alternatives.note: Add -lfsnotify; start fsevmgr in the target image.

findings.title: sleep-based periodic loop

locations.snippet: usleep(2000);                        /* slow formatting while holding the lock */

findings.guidance: A relative sleep inside a loop drifts by the loop body's run time. Use clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, ...) with a running deadline, or a pulse timer when the thread also needs to receive other events.

alternatives.note: Pulse timer when the loop also receives messages.

benefits.title: Predictable timing for time-critical work
benefits.why: motor_pid has timing-sensitive code (a periodic control loop; sleep-based periodic loop in src/main.c:55; timerfd periodic timer in src/main.c:15; and 3 more). On a general-purpose Linux kernel, exactly when that code runs depends on everything else the system is doing. QNX is a hard real-time OS: the highest-priority ready thread always runs, timers can deliver a pulse straight to the waiting thread, mutexes and message passing use priority inheritance, and run-masks can keep a core free for the critical thread, so timing stays predictable when the system is busy.
benefits.evidence_summary: a periodic control loop; sleep-based periodic loop in src/main.c:55; timerfd periodic timer in src/main.c:15; and 3 more

evidence_locations.snippet: usleep(2000);                        /* slow formatting while holding the lock */

benefits.title: A driver or service crash does not take the system down
benefits.why: motor_pid works with hardware (opens Linux device files under /dev). On Linux, device drivers run inside the kernel, so a driver bug can bring down the whole machine. In QNX the kernel only schedules, passes messages and handles interrupts; drivers and services such as motor_pid run as ordinary processes with their own memory protection. If one fails, the kernel and the other processes keep running and the failed process can be restarted.

benefits.title: Automatic detection and restart when a process dies
benefits.capability: Process-manager death notifications (and HAM where installed)
benefits.why: motor_pid relies on Linux supervision (runs as a background daemon; systemd unit / watchdog script in motor-pid.service:1). On QNX a small guardian can register for PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH and receive a kernel pulse the moment the daemon exits, then restart it with posix_spawn(); because services are isolated processes, restarting one does not disturb the others.
benefits.evidence_summary: runs as a background daemon; systemd unit / watchdog script in motor-pid.service:1

benefits.title: A path to functional-safety certification
benefits.why: motor_pid looks like embedded control or device software (a periodic control loop; opens Linux device files under /dev). If it ever has to meet a functional safety standard (automotive, industrial or medical), QNX offers a safety-certified variant of the OS, which removes a large part of the work compared with arguing the safety of a general-purpose kernel. Your own application still needs its own safety process.

benefits.title: See exactly what the system did, and when
benefits.capability: Kernel event tracing and structured system logging
benefits.why: motor_pid relies on Linux logging or /proc inspection (sleep-based periodic loop in src/main.c:55; mutex without priority inheritance in mixed-priority code in src/main.c:67). QNX's tracelogger records kernel events (thread switches, messages, interrupts) with timestamps, which shows exactly why a deadline was missed; slog2 gives fast, structured logs that stay readable after a crash.
benefits.evidence_summary: sleep-based periodic loop in src/main.c:55; mutex without priority inheritance in mixed-priority code in src/main.c:67

benefits.title: Most of the code carries over
benefits.why: QNX implements the POSIX APIs this code already relies on (threads, timers, sockets, files), so the port is about the Linux-only parts listed in the audit rather than a rewrite. The audit found 12 Linux-specific pattern(s) across 5 file(s); the readiness score is 0/100.

qnx_fit.headline: Strong fit: motor_pid does the kind of real-time, device or service work QNX is built for.
reasons: A driver or service crash does not take the system down
Automatic detection and restart when a process dies
caveats: Porting effort: 3 blocker/high finding(s) need code changes first (see the Audit tab and the step-by-step guide).
These are capabilities QNX provides, not measurements. Use the Verify tab on a QNX target before relying on timing.

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/main.c` multiplexes timers, notifications and I/O in a Linux event loop. A QNX channel replaces it: each source sends a pulse with its own code and priority, and a single receive call hands them to the thread in priority order.
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  TM["timer_create, SIGEV_PULSE"] -->|"code TIMER, prio 30"| CH(("channel"))
  W["worker thread"] -->|"MsgSendPulse, code FLUSH"| CH
  IO["ionotify on fd"] -->|"code IO"| CH
  CH --> L["MsgReceivePulse loop"]

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/motor_io.c` owns a device and a processing loop. On QNX that is naturally a resource manager: it registers /dev/motor_pid in the path space, clients use plain open/read/ write/devctl, and every request arrives as a message that inherits the client's priority. Device access moves out of client code into one process that can be restarted on its own.
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C1["client: open + devctl"] -->|"MsgSend, client priority"| R["/dev/motor_pid resource manager"]
  T["timer pulse"] --> R
  R --> D["device driver resmgr"]

pillar1_features.rationale: Background work in `src/main.c` can be given a CPU budget per replenishment period with SCHED_SPORADIC, so it cannot crowd out the time-critical loop. (Adaptive partitioning is not available in SDP 8.0; sporadic scheduling is the in-process tool.)

`motor-pid.service` relies on systemd or scripts for restarts. On QNX 8.0, procmgr_daemon() and procmgr_event_notify_add(PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH) notify a guardian via kernel pulse immediately on process termination (or use HAM when the optional HA package is installed).
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  S["motor_pid daemon"] -->|"PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH pulse"| G["procmgr / guardian"]
  G -->|"posix_spawn restart"| S

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/main.c` shares state between threads of different priorities. Priority inheritance on the mutex (or moving the shared state behind message passing, which inherits priority by default) prevents a low-priority holder from delaying the real-time thread.
`src/main.c` pins work to a CPU. QNX run-masks do this per thread and can set the mask that child threads inherit, keeping the control core free of background work.
Read each worker thread's CPU-time clock from `src/main.c` periodically (or arm a timer on it) to detect a thread that exceeds its expected budget and report or throttle it.

Capture a kernel event trace with tracelogger while motor_pid runs and inspect scheduling, IPC and interrupts in the System Profiler (Momentics or the VS Code QNX Toolkit) to confirm the timing behaviour after porting.
When motor_pid must be isolated from untrusted or heavy workloads with stronger guarantees than in-OS scheduling, run them in separate guests under the QNX Hypervisor.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: The epoll loop treats every ready descriptor equally; a burst on one fd delays the periodic work handled by the same loop.

evidence_locations.snippet: if (cfd >= 0) { ev.data.fd = cfd; epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, cfd, &ev); }

pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A channel-based loop receives pulses in priority order, so the control-timer pulse can be given a higher priority than configuration or telemetry events.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: The control loop's timing relies on a Linux-specific timerfd read inside a general-purpose event loop.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A timer that delivers a pulse wakes the control thread directly at a chosen priority. Wake-up lateness can be measured on the target with the agent's timer benchmark.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: CPU pinning uses a glibc-specific API.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: Run-masks pin the control thread and its children to a reserved core.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Device control calls are scattered through application code and tied to Linux request codes.

evidence_locations.snippet: ioctl(enc_fd, TIOCMBIS, &bits);       /* wake the encoder bridge */

pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A HAL with a devctl()-based QNX backend isolates board-specific commands in one file.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: A high-priority control thread and a low-priority thread share a default mutex. If the low-priority holder is preempted, the control thread waits indefinitely (priority inversion).
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: With PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT the holder runs at the waiter's priority until it unlocks. The agent's timer benchmark under load shows the effect on wake-up lateness.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Restart policy lives in systemd or a cron script, which QNX targets do not have.

pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: procmgr_event_notify_add(PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH) delivers a kernel pulse the instant a supervised daemon terminates so a lightweight guardian or HAM can respawn it.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Background threads have no CPU budget; a runaway worker can starve lower-priority work and delay the loop.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: SCHED_SPORADIC caps a worker's high-priority execution per period, and a CPU-time clock lets the service detect overruns.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Relative sleeps accumulate drift equal to the loop body's execution time.

evidence_locations.snippet: usleep(2000);                        /* slow formatting while holding the lock */

pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: Absolute-deadline sleeps or pulse timers keep the period fixed.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: The periodic loop's wake-up lateness under background CPU load is unknown on QNX.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: Run the agent's timer benchmark (1 kHz pulse timer, SCHED_FIFO) with and without low-priority load threads to measure wake-up lateness on your target.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Device access and client handling live in one process with the application logic.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: As a resource manager the service is a separate process that clients reach through open/read/devctl; it can be restarted without restarting its clients' code. The agent measures the time from spawn until /dev/<service> appears.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Clients exchange data with the service through Linux-specific mechanisms.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: QNX synchronous message passing copies data directly between address spaces and inherits the client's priority. The agent's IPC benchmark measures MsgSend round trips.

pillar3_steps.title: Cross-compile with the QNX 8.0 toolchain
pillar3_steps.explanation: Cross-compile with the kit's toolchain file (qcc/q++ with -V gcc_nto<arch>). Changes needed: Host-only compiler settings: Source qnxsdp-env.sh, then configure with the kit's toolchain file. Linux-only link libraries: Use Threads::Threads and drop -lrt/-ldl where the sysroot has no such library. inotify file watching: Add fsnotify to the QNX link libraries (the kit's qnx8.cmake snippet does this).
pillar3_steps.before_code:
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER gcc)
add_compile_options(-O2 -Wall -march=native)
target_link_libraries(motor_pid pthread rt m)
pillar3_steps.after_code:
# Add to motor-pid-controller's CMakeLists.txt after the target "motor_pid" is defined:
#   include(cmake/qnx8.cmake)

if(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME STREQUAL "QNX")
  target_compile_definitions(motor_pid PRIVATE _QNX_SOURCE)
  target_include_directories(motor_pid PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_LIST_DIR}/../include)
  # From the sysroot audit: fsnotify (inotify file watching)
  target_link_libraries(motor_pid fsnotify)
  # These libraries do not exist in your QNX sysroot (their functions are in libc):
  #   pthread, rt  -> remove them from target_link_libraries for QNX builds.
endif()

pillar3_steps.title: Replace the epoll loop
pillar3_steps.explanation: Start with poll() so the code builds and runs on QNX. Once it works, consider moving to a channel + pulse loop (see the resource-manager step) where each event source has its own pulse code and priority.

pillar3_steps.title: Remove sysfs dependencies
pillar3_steps.explanation: Wrap each sysfs access (PWM, thermal, GPIO) in a HAL function.
pillar3_steps.verify_command: grep -rn '"/sys/' src/  # should be empty outside hal_linux.c

pillar3_steps.title: Wrap device control in a HAL
pillar3_steps.explanation: Move ioctl() calls behind functions such as hal_set_line(); implement the QNX side with devctl().

pillar3_steps.title: Expose the service as a /dev/motor_pid resource manager
pillar3_steps.explanation: Start from the kit's resource-manager skeleton. Clients open /dev/motor_pid and use read(), write() and devctl() instead of a private socket or shared memory. The periodic work moves into the timer pulse handler, which runs serialized with client requests in one thread.

pillar3_steps.title: Replace timerfd with a pulse-delivering POSIX timer
pillar3_steps.explanation: The kit's qnx_compat.h provides qnx_periodic_timer_create()/qnx_periodic_timer_wait() built on timer_create() + SIGEV_PULSE_INIT + MsgReceivePulse(). Keep the control-loop body unchanged.

pillar3_steps.title: Pin the control thread with a run-mask
pillar3_steps.explanation: Replace sched_setaffinity() with ThreadCtl() and a run-mask.

pillar3_steps.title: Enable priority inheritance on shared mutexes
pillar3_steps.explanation: Initialize the mutex with a PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT attribute.

pillar3_steps.title: Bound background threads with SCHED_SPORADIC
pillar3_steps.explanation: Give the telemetry/worker thread a sporadic budget and low replenishment priority.

pillar3_steps.title: Use absolute-deadline sleeps for periodic work
pillar3_steps.explanation: Replace relative sleeps in periodic loops with clock_nanosleep(TIMER_ABSTIME).

pillar3_steps.title: Replace systemd supervision with startup script + procmgr death notifications
pillar3_steps.explanation: Daemonize with procmgr_daemon() and register PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH pulse notifications (or attach to HAM if installed).

Restart=always

CPUSchedulingPriority=80

pillar3_steps.verify_command: pidin -F '%a %b %N'  # on target, confirm supervised daemon running

pillar3_steps.explanation: Build the kit binaries with qcc, boot the QEMU target with mkqnximage, copy the binaries over SSH and run them under the advisor agent, which checks that the resource manager comes up and measures timer and IPC behaviour.

# QNX SDP 8.0 CMake toolchain file - generated by QNX Integration Advisor for motor-pid-controller.
# Usage:
#   source ~/qnx800/qnxsdp-env.sh
#   cmake -B build-qnx -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=cmake/qnx8-toolchain.cmake -DQNX_ARCH=x86_64
#   cmake --build build-qnx

if(NOT DEFINED ENV{QNX_TARGET} OR NOT DEFINED ENV{QNX_HOST})
  message(FATAL_ERROR "QNX_TARGET/QNX_HOST are not set. Source qnxsdp-env.sh from your SDP 8.0 install first.")
endif()

set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME QNX)
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_VERSION 8.0.0)

if(NOT DEFINED QNX_ARCH)
  set(QNX_ARCH x86_64)
endif()

if(QNX_ARCH STREQUAL "x86_64")
  set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR x86_64)
  set(_qnx_variant gcc_ntox86_64)
elseif(QNX_ARCH STREQUAL "aarch64le")
  set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR aarch64)
  set(_qnx_variant gcc_ntoaarch64le)
else()
  message(FATAL_ERROR "Unsupported QNX_ARCH '${QNX_ARCH}' (use x86_64 or aarch64le)")

set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER qcc)
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_TARGET ${_qnx_variant})
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER q++)
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_TARGET ${_qnx_variant}_cxx)

set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH $ENV{QNX_TARGET} $ENV{QNX_TARGET}/${QNX_ARCH})
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM NEVER)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY)

# Builds the QNX porting-kit binaries for motor-pid-controller.
#   source ~/qnx800/qnxsdp-env.sh && make -f Makefile.qnx ARCH=x86_64
ARCH ?= x86_64
VARIANT_x86_64    = gcc_ntox86_64
VARIANT_aarch64le = gcc_ntoaarch64le
CC      = qcc -V$(VARIANT_$(ARCH))
CFLAGS  = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=gnu11 -Iinclude -Isrc
OUT     = build/$(ARCH)

all: $(OUT)/motor_pid_resmgr $(OUT)/motor_pidctl $(OUT)/compat_selftest

$(OUT)/motor_pid_resmgr: src/qnx_motor_pid_resmgr.c src/motor_pid_dcmd.h
	mkdir -p $(OUT)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $<

$(OUT)/motor_pidctl: src/motor_pidctl.c src/motor_pid_dcmd.h
	mkdir -p $(OUT)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $<

$(OUT)/compat_selftest: tests/compat_selftest.c include/qnx_compat.h
	mkdir -p $(OUT)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $<

clean:
	rm -rf build

.PHONY: all clean

kit.description: mkqnximage QEMU target + copy binaries over SSH
kit.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Build and boot a QNX 8.0 QEMU target with mkqnximage, then copy the kit binaries to it.
# Generated by QNX Integration Advisor for motor-pid-controller.
# Prerequisites: QNX SDP 8.0 with mkqnximage, QEMU, `source qnxsdp-env.sh`, an SSH key.
# Check `mkqnximage --help` for the exact options in your SDP patch level.
set -eu

ARCH=${ARCH:-x86_64}
VM_DIR=${VM_DIR:-$HOME/qnx-advisor-vm}
SSH_PUB=${SSH_PUB:-$HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub}
KIT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)

command -v mkqnximage >/dev/null || { echo "mkqnximage not found: source qnxsdp-env.sh first" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$SSH_PUB" ] || { echo "SSH public key $SSH_PUB not found (set SSH_PUB)" >&2; exit 1; }

mkdir -p "$VM_DIR"
cd "$VM_DIR"
if [ ! -d output ]; then
    echo "== building QEMU image in $VM_DIR"
    mkqnximage --type=qemu --arch="$ARCH" --ssh-ident="$SSH_PUB"
fi

echo "== starting VM (headless)"
mkqnximage --run=-h &
sleep 5

IP=""
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
    IP=$(mkqnximage --getip 2>/dev/null || true)
    [ -n "$IP" ] && break
    sleep 2
done
[ -n "$IP" ] || { echo "could not get VM IP" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "== VM at $IP"

make -C "$KIT_DIR" -f Makefile.qnx ARCH="$ARCH"
scp -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new "$KIT_DIR"/build/"$ARCH"/* qnxuser@"$IP":/data/home/qnxuser/
echo "== copied kit binaries to /data/home/qnxuser on $IP"
echo "   ssh qnxuser@$IP"
echo "   then: su -c '/data/home/qnxuser/motor_pid_resmgr -u 1000 &' && /data/home/qnxuser/motor_pidctl"

# Advanced / optional: mkifs buildfile fragment for motor-pid-controller.
# For QEMU and VMs prefer mkqnximage (target/run-qemu.sh). Merge this fragment into a
# board buildfile from your BSP if you build a custom image.

[+script] .motor_pid-start = {
    fsevmgr &
    /proc/boot/motor_pid_resmgr -p 1 -u 1000 &
    waitfor /dev/motor_pid 5
}

[perms=0755] /proc/boot/motor_pid_resmgr = build/x86_64/motor_pid_resmgr
[perms=0755] /proc/boot/motor_pidctl = build/x86_64/motor_pidctl
